questions.enonce_markdown: Find an equation of the line $AB$, in the form $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Here $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$ is the position vector of $A$. In the stated form $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}$ the vector multiplying $t$ is a direction vector of the line; it must be the direction $\overrightarrow{AB}$, not the position vector of $B$ (the position vector $\mathbf{b}$ of $B$ is not parallel to $AB$, since $\mathbf{a}$ is not a multiple of $\mathbf{b}$, so $\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}$ would not pass through $B$).

Direction vector:
$$\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} = (-3 - 1)\mathbf{i} + (-1 - 5)\mathbf{j} + (7 + 3)\mathbf{k} = -4\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j} + 10\mathbf{k} = -2(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k}).$$
So
$$\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}) + t(-4\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j} + 10\mathbf{k}),$$
or, with a simpler direction vector and a rescaled parameter,
$$\boxed{\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}) + t(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k})}$$
Check: $t = 0$ gives $A$; with the first form $t = 1$ gives $-3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 7\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{b}$, the point $B$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, find the position vector of $M$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The position vector of the midpoint is the mean of the position vectors of the end points:
$$\overrightarrow{OM} = \frac{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}}{2} = \frac{(1 - 3)\mathbf{i} + (5 - 1)\mathbf{j} + (-3 + 7)\mathbf{k}}{2} = \frac{-2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}}{2}.$$
$$\boxed{\overrightarrow{OM} = -\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}}$$
(Check: $M$ is the point $t = \tfrac12$ on the line $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$: $\mathbf{a} + \tfrac12(-4, -6, 10) = (-1, 2, 2)$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Find the Cartesian equation of the plane $ABC$. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Two vectors in the plane:
$$\overrightarrow{AB} = (-4, -6, 10), \qquad \overrightarrow{AC} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a} = (1 - 1, 1 - 5, 0 + 3) = (0, -4, 3).$$
A normal vector is the vector product:
$$\mathbf{n} = \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -4 & -6 & 10 \\ 0 & -4 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = \big((-6)(3) - (10)(-4)\big)\mathbf{i} - \big((-4)(3) - (10)(0)\big)\mathbf{j} + \big((-4)(-4) - (-6)(0)\big)\mathbf{k}$$
$$= 22\mathbf{i} + 12\mathbf{j} + 16\mathbf{k} = 2(11\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} + 8\mathbf{k}).$$
Take $\mathbf{n} = 11\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} + 8\mathbf{k}$. The plane is $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}$ with $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 11 + 30 - 24 = 17$:
$$\boxed{11x + 6y + 8z = 17}$$
Check with the other points: $B$: $-33 - 6 + 56 = 17$; $C$: $11 + 6 + 0 = 17$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Find the value of the constant $a$ for which the line $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k} + \lambda(2\mathbf{i} + a\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})$ is parallel to the plane $ABC$. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A line is parallel to a plane when its direction vector is perpendicular to the normal of the plane. The direction vector is $\mathbf{d} = 2\mathbf{i} + a\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ and the normal of the plane $ABC$ is $\mathbf{n} = 11\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} + 8\mathbf{k}$ (here $a$ is the unknown constant, not the position vector $\mathbf{a}$). Require $\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$:
$$2(11) + 6a + 1(8) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; 22 + 6a + 8 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; 6a = -30.$$
$$\boxed{a = -5}$$
The line does not lie in the plane: its point $(0, 1, 2)$ gives $11(0) + 6(1) + 8(2) = 22 \ne 17$, so for $a = -5$ the line is parallel to the plane and distinct from it.
